title: Culvert Nine
passages:
The dot on the movement trace kept walking, ahead of the cart, steady as a meter tick. Kass gripped the cart handles and looked up the grade. The rails ran dark into the cut, no headlight, no plate, just the shape of a ghost train eating the ore line toward them.

"Ghost," Kass said. "Plate stripped. It won't answer hails."

Ospina shifted the seal die in their pocket. "It won't stop for bodies on the rail either."

"We're not asking it to stop for bodies," Kass said. "We're asking it to check for a flag."

The old flag was a length of relay orange tied to a broken surveyor's pole. Kass planted it in the sleeper ties, stepped onto the rail with Ospina, and waved it hard. The cart's wheels squeaked against the steel. Far up the grade, the train's air brakes hissed once—a soft check, like it noticed, like it cared—and then the hiss stopped. The rig did not slow. It did not stop. Ghost trains drove themselves between nodes; they had no crew to see a flag, no brake handle for a person to pull.

"Into the cut," Kass said.

They hauled the cart off the rail and dragged it into the drainage cut beside the grade, metal scraping on rock. The train screamed past, a wall of dark steel and displaced air that shoved the cart sideways and left the rail humming. Kass stayed flat until the rumble faded into the dark. Their ears were ringing. The cart had tipped onto one wheel, its load of empty crates rattling.

Then the dot from the movement trace stepped onto the road.

It was a person, wrapped in a Culvert Nine coat, carrying a hand lamp and a clipboard. They stopped ten paces away and looked at the empty cart.

"Two of you," the lookout said. Their voice was dry, sharp enough to cut grease. "Cart's empty. You came down-line for cargo and brought nothing back."

"We were waiting for a train that doesn't stop for people," Kass said. "Who are you?"

"Lookout. Brill's crew. I count the heads that walk my road." The lookout tapped the clipboard. "You're Kass. Dispatcher, post 71. Ospina. Seal authority, bay four. You're down from Anza with a red plate and no resupply."

Ospina's hand stayed on their pocket. "Brill's crew. You hoard the skim."

"We eat it," the lookout said. "Brill's people have been drawing rations off the totalizer all night while Anza starves. Every seal you're missing went through this station. Every calorie."

The totalizer was the station meter that counted stock out of the storeroom by receiving mark. If Brill's crew had been drawing against it, the food wasn't lost—it was earmarked, already eaten by someone else's winter.

"Where is Brill?" Kass asked.

"Back room. With the man who made the seals hot." The lookout stepped aside, lamp swinging. "You want the scrubbers? You want Anza eating past dawn? You talk to Voss. And you bring something to trade. Brill doesn't take promises. She takes stock."

The lookout turned and walked back toward the pump station, leaving Kass and Ospina with the empty cart and the dark grade. Somewhere ahead, the ghost train had vanished down the ore line, plate-less and unlogged, while Culvert Nine ate Anza's eleven seals one ration at a time.

The pump house sat at the bottom of a dry sump, its door hung crooked on one hinge, and they went in past a turbine the size of a rail car that hadn't turned since the water left the Interior. Inside it smelled like dust, cold oil, and bread.

Then the lamp found the crates.

They were stacked the length of the pump hall, pallet on pallet, every one of them ringed in chalk: *Br-4*. Cornmeal in fifty-pound sacks. Fuse wire on wooden spools, enough to rewire a relay shop twice. Canned milk three tiers deep with the labels sun-bleached to the color of weak tea. And on the low pallet by the sump grate, six cases with an Anza relay shop routing tag still wired to the handles—scrubber cartridges, the kind that pull carbon back out of a breath so a man doesn't have to work for every lungful he takes.

Kass crouched at the low pallet and counted the cases out loud. Twice. As if the number might improve.

"Four restarts," Ospina said. "Rhea's got four restarts and a hand pump."

"Then she'd better keep pumping," a woman said from the stair.

She came down slow, a short woman in a receiver's coat with the cuffs cut off, a hand lamp in one fist and nothing in the other. Behind her the lookout set the clipboard on a nail and stayed by the door.

"Brill," Kass said.

"You walked my road and read my chalk. I'm not going to pretend to be somebody else." Brill put her lamp on a crate lid so it lit all of them at once. "That's Anza's winter on my floor. Cornmeal, milk, fuse wire. I know exactly whose it is. I've known since the second run came in."

"Then hand it over," Ospina said.

"No."

Ospina's jaw worked. "You've got our food, our wire, and eleven seals' worth of Anza's roster, and you're going to stand there and tell me no."

"I'm going to stand here and tell you the rule, and then you can be as angry as you like about it." Brill didn't raise her voice. "Nothing leaves this hall without a trade. Not a sack. Not a cartridge."

Saul spoke from the door, tapping the clipboard. "The totalizer's a brass wheel behind glass. Every case that crosses that chalk line, I strike the receiving mark on the tally and the wheel turns. No power in this station and it still counts. That's the whole point of it." They shrugged. "Nine people eat off that wheel. Two of them are mine."

"Nine," Kass said. "You've got nine people and a pump station's worth of Anza's resupply."

"I've got nine people and a road that gets walked by things with no plate on them, dispatcher. Don't talk to me about hoarding."

"I'm not talking about hoarding. I'm talking about a man at Anza relay shop breathing on a rubber disc and a hand pump, on a node with a red plate and a frozen line."

"Everybody's got a man," Brill said. "I had a storeroom once, at a real station with a real line behind it. A man with a clean voice and a full clipboard took four crates off my floor and left me a promise written on line paper. I ate the paper. It was terrible." She picked her lamp back up. "I trust a full storeroom over any person's word, and I've earned that. My people eat through winter off this pile, or they don't eat. That's not cruelty, that's arithmetic."

"Arithmetic," Ospina said. "You've got four crates of arithmetic sitting there that were routed to a relay shop."

"Then buy them."

Kass stood up. "With what? You've seen our plate. We came down-line with an empty cart because a ghost train doesn't stop for people, and you counted us at the door."

"I don't take promises," Brill said. "I take stock, and I take trades. Bring me something I can stack."

Behind her, deeper in the station, something hissed. Then a clunk. Then, patient as a pump that still had water in it, the hiss and the clunk again.

Saul didn't look up from the tally. "That's been going since midnight."

"That's the man who made your seals hot," Brill said. "He's the only one under this roof with a trade you can afford."
